Neonates of the Alligator snapping turtle emerge from leathery-shelled eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 30.5 °C [T = 30.5 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 120 days [ab = approximately 120 days]. Upon hatching, which involves the use of an egg caruncle to break the parchment-like shell, the hatchlings possess a carapace length at birth of about 3 centimeters [Lb = about 3 centimeters]. This modest size at emergence, characteristic of many chelonians, belies the substantial growth potential of the species. The initial yolk-sac larva stage is brief, as the young turtles quickly absorb their endogenous yolk reserves and commence a lecithotrophic existence before transitioning to active feeding. During this early phase, the tiny individuals are vulnerable to a wide array of aquatic predators, including large fish and wading birds, which exerts strong selective pressure for rapid early development. Field surveys of nesting sites along river systems in the southeastern United States have confirmed these incubation parameters, noting that even minor fluctuations in nest temperature can significantly alter hatching success and offspring phenotype.

The species is renowned for attaining some of the largest body sizes among freshwater turtles, with comprehensive surveys of adult populations yielding a maximum recorded carapace length of 80.8 centimeters [Li = 80.8 centimeters]. This ultimate carapace length represents the asymptotic size approached by the oldest and most dominant individuals, particularly males who continue slow somatic growth throughout their lives. Complementary data on body mass reveal that such large adults can achieve an ultimate wet weight of up to 58500 grams [Wwi = up to 58500 grams], although anecdotal historical accounts from the early twentieth century occasionally report specimens exceeding 80 kilograms. Sexual dimorphism is pronounced in this species, with males regularly surpassing females in both linear dimensions and overall mass. The attainment of such massive size is facilitated by a sedentary, ambush-predation lifestyle and a remarkably low metabolic rate, which allows the turtles to channel most assimilated energy into somatic tissue rather than costly activity. Comparative analyses with other members of the family Chelydridae suggest that Macrochelys temminckii exhibits the highest degree of gigantism within the clade.

Female Alligator snapping turtles undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching reproductive maturity, with puberty occurring at a carapace length of approximately 33 centimeters [Lp = approximately 33 centimeters]. This length serves as a reliable morphological indicator of the onset of gonadal activity in females, though males typically mature at a slightly smaller size. At this stage of development, the wet weight at puberty for females is around 8000 grams [Wwp = around 8000 grams], reflecting the substantial investment in body reserves necessary to support future reproductive efforts. The transition from juvenile to sexually mature adult involves a suite of hormonal and physiological changes, including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Field studies employing mark-recapture techniques have demonstrated that females in populations with abundant prey resources, such as those inhabiting alluvial rivers in Louisiana and Mississippi, reach this size threshold at a younger age than conspecifics in more oligotrophic environments. The sub-adult growth phase is characterized by a gradual decline in the annual growth rate as resources are increasingly diverted towards the development of reproductive tissues rather than skeletal expansion.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], longitudinal studies have documented that the time since birth at puberty for females is approximately 4015 days [tp = approximately 4015 days], a protracted juvenile period that ranks among the longest documented for North American freshwater turtles and reflects the species’ extremely slow life-history pace. At this same thermal regime of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Alligator snapping turtle has been estimated at approximately 70.3 years [am = approximately 70.3 years], based on recapture data of long-term captive individuals and validated through skeletal growth annuli analysis. The combination of late sexual maturation and exceptional longevity is characteristic of a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over early reproductive output. Such a strategy is adaptive in stable, resource-predictable environments where the risk of juvenile mortality is high but adult mortality is low. These demographic parameters position Macrochelys temminckii as a quintessential K-selected species within the chelonian lineage.

The maximum reproductive rate of the Alligator snapping turtle has been quantified in nesting surveys conducted under a sustained water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], revealing that females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] containing an average of approximately 30 eggs [N_R_i = containing an average of approximately 30 eggs]. This low frequency of reproduction, combined with high egg and hatchling mortality, means that only a tiny fraction of offspring survive to replace the parents in the population. Conservation assessments have therefore emphasized the vulnerability of this species to any increase in adult mortality rates, whether from bycatch in commercial fishing gear or from illegal harvesting for the exotic pet trade. The reproductive ecology of the Alligator snapping turtle exemplifies the trade-offs inherent in a life-history strategy that allocates resources preferentially to somatic maintenance and longevity rather than to immediate high fecundity.
